The irreversible anthropogenic perturbation of the Earth's biophysical systems (Witze, 2024), manifest in geomorphological transformations (Nixon, 2011), has garnered terminological acknowledgment through the neologism 'Anthropocene' (Moore, 2016), initially proposed by Stoermer and Crutzen in 2000 (Nixon, 2011). Their revision of geological nomenclature (Smith & Zeder, 2013) entails the introduction of the 'Anthropocene epoch', intended to supplant the Holocene epoch (Haraway, 2016), thereby emphasizing the unprecedented biophysical dominance exerted by the Anthropos from the onset of the industrial era (Nixon, 2011). This paradigmatic shift in geological thought (Barnosky et al., 2011) underscores the profound impact of human activities on the Earth's biophysical systems, precipitating a new era of anthropogenic influence (Witze, 2024). The Anthropocene epoch, as a proposed geological epoch, seeks to rectify the lacuna in our understanding of the Earth's history, highlighting the transformative power of human activities on the planet's biophysical systems (Moore, 2016). By adopting this new nomenclature, scientists aim to underscore the significance of human-induced changes in the Earth's biophysical systems, thereby fostering a more nuanced comprehension of the complex relationships between human societies and the natural environment (Haraway, 2016).
